sections.section_title: Background and Pathophysiology of Heparin‑Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) and Autoimmune HIT
sections.description: This section reviews the fundamental mechanisms by which heparin exposure leads to platelet‑activating antibodies, the classic HIT pathway, and the emerging concept of autoimmune HIT (aHIT) with heparin‑independent platelet activation. It highlights the unique clinical features, timing, and laboratory distinctions between classic and autoimmune HIT, providing the necessary foundation to understand the patient’s presentation and diagnostic strategy.
subtopics: Heparin exposure and platelet factor 4 (PF4) release during cardiac surgery
Formation of PF4/heparin immune complexes and IgG antibody generation
Classic HIT: timing, FcγRIIa‑mediated platelet activation, thrombosis risk
Autoimmune HIT: heparin‑independent platelet activation, high‑affinity anti‑PF4 antibodies
Clinical spectrum of aHIT: severe thrombocytopenia, early onset, thrombotic events
Diagnostic testing overview: PF4/polyanion ELISA, serotonin‑release assay (SRA)
Key laboratory distinctions between classic HIT and aHIT

sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Workup
sections.description: This section narrates the patient’s demographic and procedural background, the rapid decline in platelet counts, neurologic changes, and the laboratory workup performed on postoperative day five. It sets the stage for the differential diagnosis by detailing the timing, laboratory values, and exclusion of common postoperative causes of thrombocytopenia.
subtopics: Patient demographics and comorbidities (atrial fibrillation, apixaban)
Pre‑operative cardiac catheterisation with low‑dose UFH
Intra‑operative heparin dosing and cardiopulmonary bypass details
Post‑operative platelet trend: POD1 155, POD5 50, POD6 26, POD7 13
Development of delirium and CT‑confirmed left parietal stroke
Laboratory profile on POD5: CBC, coagulation panel, fibrinogen, d‑dimer, haptoglobin, cultures
Exclusion of other causes: bleeding, infection, DIC, TTP, transfusion reactions

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Clinical Reasoning for HIT
sections.description: This section walks through the systematic exclusion of common postoperative causes of thrombocytopenia and explains why HIT remained the most plausible diagnosis. It discusses the relevance of early (< POD5) platelet decline, prior UFH exposure, and the presence of a thrombotic event.
subtopics: Common postoperative causes of thrombocytopenia: shock, sepsis, DIC, TTP, drug reactions, transfusion reactions
Early onset (< POD5) platelet drop and its diagnostic significance
Prior intra‑operative UFH exposure during catheterisation as a trigger
Thrombotic stroke supporting a hypercoagulable state
Application of the 4‑Ts score and risk stratification
Decision to pursue HIT antibody testing based on clinical suspicion

sections.section_title: Laboratory Confirmation and Interpretation of Heparin‑Induced Thrombocytopenia Antibody Assays
sections.description: This section delves into the serological tests performed, their principles, and the interpretation of the patient’s atypical serotonin‑release assay (SRA) profile. It explains how the results confirm autoimmune HIT, including the novel partial inhibition by FcγRIIa blockade.
subtopics: PF4/polyanion ELISA: principle, sensitivity, strong positive OD 2.2
Serotonin‑release assay methodology and heparin concentration response curves
Classic HIT SRA pattern vs aHIT pattern: heparin‑dependent vs independent activation
Patient’s SRA: strong release at 0, 0.1, 0.3 U/mL; complete inhibition at 100 U/mL
Partial inhibition by IV.3 monoclonal antibody: significance and novelty
Serial SRA testing showing shift toward heparin‑dependent profile over time
Integration of serology with clinical context to confirm aHIT

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Management and Monitoring in Autoimmune HIT
sections.description: This section outlines the step‑by‑step treatment plan: cessation of fondaparinux, initiation of argatroban, administration of high‑dose intravenous immunoglobulin, monitoring of coagulation markers, transition to fondaparinux, antithrombin supplementation, and resumption of apixaban. It explains the rationale for each decision and the indicators used to guide therapy.
subtopics: Anticoagulant options in HIT: direct thrombin inhibitors, factor Xa inhibitors, heparin alternatives
Initial use of argatroban: safety in recent stroke, short half‑life
High‑dose intravenous immunoglobulin: dosing, expected platelet recovery kinetics
Monitoring of fibrinogen, d‑dimer, schistocytes, and platelet count
Criteria for switching from argatroban to fondaparinux: administration convenience, hypercoagulability control
Antithrombin supplementation before fondaparinux initiation
Long‑term anticoagulation: re‑initiation of apixaban at 5 mg BID

sections.section_title: Outcomes, Follow‑Up, and Clinical Lessons Learned
sections.description: This section summarizes the patient’s recovery trajectory, the long‑term evolution of the SRA profile, and the key clinical take‑aways. It emphasizes the importance of recognizing early-onset aHIT, interpreting atypical laboratory results, and tailoring anticoagulation strategies to prevent morbidity.
subtopics: Platelet recovery: nadir 13, 155 at POD62, 202 at POD87
Neuroimaging: resolution of parietal stroke and full neurological recovery
Long‑term SRA evolution: shift from aHIT to classic HIT over 4 months
Clinical significance of pre‑operative UFH exposure and early onset aHIT
Novel laboratory profile: partial IV.3 inhibition and diagnostic implications
Hypercoagulability markers: fibrinogen decline, d‑dimer rise, schistocytes
Practical recommendations: early HIT work‑up post‑cardiac surgery, interpreting atypical SRA, use of IVIG, choice of anticoagulant
